paperInfo.subject: Agric, Science & Tech
paperInfo.paperName: Grade 7 Agric, Science & Tech — Paper 2 (Practice Set B)

questions.questionText: SECTION A (30 marks - answer ALL questions, about 75 minutes). Question 1 (5 marks): (a) What does the term 'agriculture' mean? [1]. (b) Give any two types of farming scale practised in Zimbabwe [2]. (c) Give any one horticultural cash crop grown in Zimbabwe [1]. (d) State one way in which agriculture is important to a country's economy [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Meaning of agriculture:** The **art, science, and economic practice of cultivating soil to produce useful crops AND rearing domestic livestock** (alongside forestry and fisheries) to provide human food, fibre, cash income, and industrial raw materials [1 mark]. **(b) Two scales of farming practised in Zimbabwe:** **Subsistence (communal) farming** (producing primarily to feed the family first), **Small-scale commercial / A1/A2 farming**, **Large-scale commercial farming**, or **Co-operative farming** [2 marks]. **(c) One Zimbabwean horticultural cash crop:** **Paprika, tomatoes, green beans/mange-tout peas, roses/cut flowers, citrus oranges, or avocados** [1 mark]. **(d) Economic importance to Zimbabwe:** Agriculture **earns vital foreign currency** through high-value tobacco, horticulture, and cotton exports, creates **jobs** for millions across rural farms and factories, supplies **raw materials** (sugar, cotton lint, timber) to local industries, and guarantees **national food security** [1 mark].

Horticulture specifically focuses on high-value intensive garden crops—fresh vegetables, fruits, ornamental flowers, and herbs—requiring closer irrigation, grading, and cold-chain marketing than broad field grain maize!

Keep **Crop production + Livestock rearing** BOTH inside your 1-mark definition of agriculture, and always name a true **horticultural** cash crop (fruit/veg/flowers/spices) rather than maize or wheat in part (c)!

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) Give any two reasons why farmers add fertiliser to their soil [2]. (b) State three nutrients needed by plants in large amounts (macronutrients) [3]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Two reasons farmers add fertiliser to soil:** to **replenish essential mineral nutrients** continuously exported off fields by previous harvests or leached down by rain, and to **boost healthy rapid plant growth, correct visible nutrient deficiency yellowing, and lift both harvest yield and market quality** [2 marks]. **(b) Three major plant macronutrients (N-P-K):** **Nitrogen (N)** (drives lush green vegetative leaf growth and protein formation), **Phosphorus (P)** (builds vigorous deep early root systems, sturdy stems, flowering, and seed ripening), and **Potassium (K)** (strengthens general plant disease hardiness, water regulation, fruit sweetness, and stalk strength) [3 marks].

Remember that Compound D basal fertiliser placed near planting supplies balanced **Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium** to launch strong roots early, whereas **Ammonium Nitrate (AN)** is added later as **Nitrogen-rich top-dressing** when tall leafy maize hits knee-height!

Always spell all three primary macronutrients accurately (**Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium** — matching the N-P-K numbers printed on every Zimbabwean fertiliser bag!) and distinguish macronutrients cleanly from micronutrients (*boron, zinc, iron*) needed in tiny traces.

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) Give any three causes of soil pollution [3]. (b) The diagram below shows a simplified water cycle. Label the processes marked A and B: Clouds form and grow heavy, then release rain that falls to the ground (process A - the falling of moisture from clouds to the ground); the sun heats water on the ground/rivers/lakes, turning it into water vapour that rises into the air (process B - water turning into vapour and rising). Name process A and process B [2]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Three causes of soil pollution:** **careless dumping of non-biodegradable plastics and household litter**, accidental **agrochemical/pesticide spills** or excessive overuse of toxic chemical sprays, **leaking motor oil/industrial chemical wastes**, and untreated sewage sludge dumped onto farmland [3 marks]. **(b) Simplified Water Cycle processes:** **Process A is Precipitation** (heavy condensed cloud water droplets or hail falling downward out of clouds onto farmland and rivers under gravity) [1 mark]; **Process B is Evaporation** (solar heat energy warming liquid surface water on dams, rivers, and wet soil into invisible rising **water vapour**) [1 mark].

Understanding both halves protects farm water sustainably: **precipitation** brings vital seasonal rain cleanly down onto pastures, yet careless **plastic, pesticide, and oil pollution** resting on topsoil gets washed straight into rivers and boreholes the moment storm water runs!

Check directional arrows carefully in Paper 2 water-cycle diagrams: **A (Clouds → Ground = Precipitation)**, **B (Ground/River → Air = Evaporation)**, and remember **Transpiration** adds extra vapour upward from leafy green plants too!

questions.questionText: (5 marks): A farmer is growing a crop with a tall central stem, long narrow leaves, a tassel at the top, and cobs growing partway up the stem, with fibrous roots at the base. (a)(i) Which crop is being described? [1]. (ii) What is the function of the tassel at the top of the plant? [1]. (iii) Give one function of the fibrous roots [1]. (b) In Zimbabwe, this crop is normally grown in which season? [2]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a)(i) Crop described:** **Maize** (*Zea mays*—Zimbabwe’s staple tall cereal grass matching narrow parallel-veined leaves, top male tassel, mid-stem female cobs, and fibrous root crown) [1 mark]. **(ii) Function of the top tassel:** produces and sheds huge clouds of light yellow **pollen grains** (carried cleanly by wind onto receptive sticky cob **silks** below) so **pollination and fertilisation** occur and full maize kernels develop on the cob [1 mark]. **(iii) One function of fibrous roots:** **absorb water and dissolved soil mineral salts** upward into the stalk, **anchor the tall top-heavy maize plant upright** against gusty summer winds, and weave upper topsoil together helping reduce erosion [1 mark]. **(b) Growing season in Zimbabwe:** grown predominantly during the **Summer Rainy Season** (typically planted early with first effective rains around **October–December** and harvested mature in dry April–June, except small winter green-mealie irrigated frost-free valleys) [2 marks].

Notice why mid-season January droughts at *tasselling and silking* wreck maize harvests so dramatically: dry burning heat dries sticky silks before wind-blown tassel pollen fertilises ovules, leaving sad empty toothless cobs!

Distinguish clearly in Paper 2 between the maize **male flower (tassel at apex producing pollen)** and **female flower (silks emerging from ears/cobs receiving pollen)**.

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) List the two classes of farm animals based on where they are kept/how they are managed [2]. (b) Mr Chikwanha keeps goats on his farm. (i) His female goats are producing very little milk. Which nutrient class should be increased in their feed to boost milk production? [1]. (ii) Give one reason why goats are important to Mr Chikwanha's household [1]. Total: give one more general reason livestock are valued in rural Zimbabwean households [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Two management classes of farm animals:** **Domestic (tame home-kept) animals** bred and fed carefully under human care (cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, broilers, donkeys) versus **Wild animals** roaming freely in natural savanna habitats or managed wildlife reserves (impala, kudu, ostriches, lions, elephants) [2 marks]. **(b)(i) Nutrient needed to boost goat milk:** **Proteins**—adding protein-rich concentrates, legume hay (like lucerne/cowpea haulms), or groundnut cake builds casein milk protein and multiplies daily milk litres cleanly [1 mark]. **(ii) Importance to Mr Chikwanha’s household & broader community [2 marks]:** goats supply Mr Chikwanha’s family directly with **fresh nutritious meat, milk, quick emergency cash from livestock sales, and rich kraal manure** for vegetable beds [1 mark]; broadly across rural Zimbabwean homesteads, livestock also serve as living **savings/wealth stores ("walking bank")**, traditional **lobola (*roora*) and cultural ceremonies**, loan collateral, and ox/donkey **draught ploughing power** [1 mark].

Hardy indigenous **Mashona / Matabele goats** thrive famously across dry Regions IV and V because goats browse thorny shrubs gracefully when dry grass turns scarce, rebounding quickly for smallholders!

Answer every single micro-part clearly labelled: **(a) Domestic vs Wild**, **(b)(i) Protein**, **(b)(ii) direct household benefit + broader socio-economic livestock role** (noting **zero marks** get skipped when reading 5-mark totals carefully!).

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) Where on a farm should equipment and machinery be stored when not in use? [1]. (b) Name any two hand tools commonly used on a farm [2]. (c) To keep track of tools on the farm, a farmer should keep a ___________ [1]. (d) How can a farmer maintain a tool with moving/rotating parts, such as a wheelbarrow or plough disc? [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Safe tool/machinery storage place:** inside a **dry, lockable, shaded roofed tool storeroom or implement shed** elevated safely off damp soil so rain and sun never rust blades or rot wooden handles [1 mark]. **(b) Two common hand tools:** **Hoe (badza)** for weeding/ridging, **spade/shovel** for turning soil/loading manure, **garden rake** for levelling fine seedbeds, **sickle/slasher** for cutting tall grass, or **hand trowel** for transplanting seedlings [2 marks]. **(c) Missing record-book blank:** an **Inventory / Tool & Equipment Register** logging exact tool numbers, issue dates, and borrower names [1 mark]. **(d) Maintaining moving/rotating parts:** wipe dirt clean, apply fresh **oil or lubricating grease** onto bearings, axles, wheel hubs, and disc joints regularly to **slash metal-on-metal friction, stop wear, and seal damp rust away** [1 mark].

Hanging painted hoes, spades, and forks neatly on wall hooks after scraping mud dry off blades stops sharp tools from cluttering shed floors where workers might step on blades and injure feet!

Check the 1-mark blank in (c): always write the exact management term **Inventory (or Equipment/Asset Register)**—plus explain **why** oil/grease helps moving wheels (**reduces friction + prevents rust**).

questions.questionText: SECTION B (20 marks - answer any TWO of Questions 7 to 10, about 45 minutes). Question 7 (10 marks): Choose ONE leaf vegetable crop and describe how it is grown, using the following headings. (a) Name of the crop [1]. (b) Land preparation (two steps) [2]. (c) Planting (two steps) [2]. (d) Weeding (two methods) [2]. (e) Harvesting (two steps) [2]. (f) Give one pest that attacks this crop [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [10 marks]:** **(a) Selected leaf vegetable crop:** **Rape (*Brassica napus*) / Covo / Kale** [1 mark]. **(b) Land preparation (2 clear steps):** **(1)** Clear weeds, stones, and tough grass stubs, then dig deeply (~20–25 cm) with a fork/hoe breaking big clods; **(2)** Mix in well-rotted **kraal manure or compost**, shape neat flat **1 m–1.2 m wide beds** cleanly, and rake top tilth smooth and level [2 marks]. **(c) Planting (2 clear steps):** **(1)** Sow clean rape seeds thinly along **1–2 cm shallow drills spaced 30–40 cm apart** (or transplant sturdy 4–6-leaf nursery seedlings cleanly 30 cm apart in moist soil during cool late afternoon); **(2)** Cover lightly with fine soil/thin grass mulch and **water gently immediately** [2 marks]. **(d) Weeding (2 methods):** **(1)** Regular **shallow hand-hoeing / hand-pulling weeds between rows** carefully without slicing surface roots; **(2)** Spreading dry **grass mulch** cleanly between plants to smother germinating weed seedlings (or approved selective pre-emergence controls commercially) [2 marks]. **(e) Harvesting (2 clear steps):** **(1)** Pluck only the **firm outer mature lower leaves cleanly upward/downward by hand**, deliberately leaving the central **growing crown intact** to keep sprouting fresh leaves for months; **(2)** Sort fresh unblemished leaves, wash in clean water, and **tie neat market bundles** in cool shade [2 marks]. **(f) Common rape pest:** **Aphids (*Brevicoryne*)** or **Diamondback moth caterpillars / Cutworms** [1 mark].

Leaving the delicate central shoot intact while harvesting older lower leaves transforms one well-fed rape bed into a continuous weekly kitchen and market cash earner for 3–5 months!

Follow the exact **six lettered headings (a) through (f)** given in Section B cleanly—marking schemes allocate **strictly 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10 marks** along those six headings!

questions.questionText: (10 marks): Describe the production of poultry (broilers) under the following headings. (a) Name of the bird being reared [2]. (b) Care of the bird (two aspects) [4]. (c) List any two products, and any two by-products, obtained from this bird [4]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [10 marks]:** **(a) Bird being reared:** **Broiler chicken** (fast-growing meat chicken hybrids such as Cobb 500 or Ross 308 reaching slaughter weight in **5–7 weeks**) [2 marks]. **(b) Care of broiler chickens (2 detailed aspects):** **(1) Housing, Warmth & Strict Hygiene:** provide a clean, dry, well-ventilated, draught-free poultry house floored with 7–10 cm of dry clean wood-shaving **deep litter** (turning wet spots promptly and cleaning/disinfecting strictly between batches) plus **brooder heat lamps/charcoal heaters (~32–34°C initially)** warming fragile day-old chicks steadily downward weekly [2 marks]; **(2) Nutrition, Fresh Water & Preventive Health:** feed age-matched high-protein **Broiler Starter → Grower → Finisher mash/pellets** round-the-clock alongside spotless cool clean drinking water in raised bell-drinkers, paired with strict **Newcastle & Gumboro vaccinations** and quiet footbath biosecurity [2 marks]. **(c) Two products & two by-products [4 marks]:** **Primary Products:** **fresh dressed broiler chicken meat** (whole birds/cuts) plus nutritious **edible giblets/offal (liver, gizzard)** *(note carefully: table **eggs** are the primary product of **layer hens**, whereas broilers are slaughtered young purely for tender meat!)*. **Valuable By-Products:** rich nitrogen-heavy **poultry litter manure** (prized garden fertiliser) and clean **feathers** (processed commercially into high-protein feather meal or pillow stuffing) [4 marks].

Catching this subtle distinction earns huge examiner respect: broilers rarely live long enough to lay eggs—their economic output is rapid lean **meat**, whereas spent litter manure and feathers provide zero-waste **by-products**!

Give rich operational steps under **(b)**—don't just write two words *"feed and water"*; specify **broiler starter/grower/finisher progression, brooder brooding warmth, deep-litter hygiene, and vaccinations**.

questions.questionText: (10 marks): The diagram shows a layered compost heap, with alternating layers of plant/animal waste materials. (a) Write any three materials used to make a compost heap [3]. (b) Give one reason why the top of the compost heap should be kept moist/covered [1]. (c) State any two ways (besides composting) of increasing soil fertility [2]. (d) Name any two materials that make up soil [2]. (e) Give one visible sign of soil erosion [1]. (f) What is the importance of using compost on a farm? [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [10 marks]:** **(a) Three compost heap materials:** **dry brown grass / chopped maize stalks** (supplying airy carbon), **fresh green vegetable peelings / green weeds without seeds**, and **animal kraal/chicken dung** (plus thin sprinkles of **garden topsoil & wood ash**) [3 marks]. **(b) Why keep compost moist & covered:** helpful **decomposer bacteria and fungi need steady moisture and mild warmth** to stay active digesting tough stalks—letting the top bake bone-dry halts decomposition dead, whereas covering with grass/sheeting slows evaporation and keeps heavy rain from washing soluble nutrients away [1 mark]. **(c) Two other ways to improve soil fertility:** **crop rotation including nitrogen-fixing legumes** (beans/groundnuts) alongside incorporating cured **farmyard kraal manure** (or ploughing crop residues cleanly and applying **lime/fertiliser** carefully) [2 marks]. **(d) Two core components making up natural soil:** weathered **mineral rock particles** (sand, silt, clay), **organic matter (humus)**, **soil water**, and **soil air** [2 marks]. **(e) Visible sign of soil erosion:** **deep cut stormwater gullies**, tiny flat-topped **"soil pedestals"** protected under pebbles, **exposed tree/maize roots**, or muddy brown silt-choked runoff [1 mark]. **(f) Why compost matters to farms:** turns free farm & kitchen trash cleanly into rich organic **soil humus and slow-release plant nutrients**, restoring moisture retention and soil structure sustainably while slashing costly mineral fertiliser purchases [1 mark].

Notice how all four soil ingredients in **(d)** stay roughly balanced inside ideal loam topsoil: about **45% mineral grit, 5% organic humus, 25% water, and 25% pore air**!

Check each micro-part carefully—especially **(d) materials making up soil** (*mineral particles, organic matter/humus, air, water*)—avoid listing litter like plastic or rubbish as a natural soil component!

questions.questionText: (10 marks): (a) Give any three reasons why agriculture is considered a business [3]. (b) The table below shows a farmer's trading record for March. Complete the table by calculating the missing values A, B and C, then find the total income (D), total expenditure (E), and the profit or loss made. INCOME: 25 trays of eggs = $150,00 | Butternuts = $70,00 | 15kg tomatoes = $45,00 | 80 heads of cabbage at 60c per head = $A | 30kg carrots = $60,00 | 40 broilers = $280,00 | 15 trays of eggs = $90,00 | 50 heads of rape at 40c per head = $B. EXPENDITURE: Chick starter mesh = $110,00 | 5 bags of grower mesh at $28,00 per bag = $C | Tomato seed = $65,00 | Fertiliser = $95,00 | Pesticides = $140,00 | Bean seed = $55,00. (i) Calculate A, B, C, total income (D) and total expenditure (E) [7 marks - 5 for the table values, allocated across the calculation]. (ii) Calculate the profit or loss made [part of the 10 marks, combined with (i)]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer & Verified Trading Account [10 marks]:** **(a) Three reasons agriculture is a genuine business:** **(1) Profit motive & budgeting**—farmers invest start-up capital planning expected yields and market revenues to earn net **profit**; **(2) Buying production inputs & selling market outputs**—purchasing seed/feed/fertiliser cleanly at input prices and grading/marketing produce to buyers; and **(3) Record-keeping, financial risk & foreign-currency trade**—tracking income vs expenditure ledgers accurately to avoid losses and grow farm wealth [3 marks].

**(b) Completed March Trading Account Calculations [7 marks]:**
- **A (80 cabbages @ 60c = $0.60 each):** 80 × $0.60 = **$48.00**
- **B (50 rape bundles @ 40c = $0.40 each):** 50 × $0.40 = **$20.00**
- **C (5 bags grower mash @ $28.00):** 5 × $28.00 = **$140.00**
- **Total Income (D):** $150.00 + $70.00 + $45.00 + $48.00 (A) + $60.00 + $280.00 + $90.00 + $20.00 (B) = **$763.00**
- **Total Expenditure (E):** $110.00 + $140.00 (C) + $65.00 + $95.00 + $140.00 + $55.00 = **$605.00**
- **Net Farm Profit/Loss:** Since Income (**$763.00**) exceeds Expenditure (**$605.00**), **Profit = $763.00 − $605.00 = $158.00 PROFIT**!

Double-check those cents conversions carefully (60c = $0.60, 40c = $0.40, NOT $60 or $40!) and add every line twice downward ($150+$70+$45+$48+$60+$280+$90+$20 = $763) and upward ($20+$90+... = $763) before labelling **$158.00 PROFIT** explicitly!

questions.questionText:
A learner compares transparent, translucent and opaque materials.
- (a) Define transparent. [1 mark]
- (b) Give one example of an opaque material. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain how shadows form. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of transparent:** A material that allows **nearly all incident light rays to pass straight through clearly without scattering**, enabling objects behind it to be seen sharply—for example **clear window glass, clean still water, or clear perspex** [1 mark]. **(b) One opaque material:** **wood, brick wall, solid sheet metal, cardboard, or stone** (blocks all light completely) [1 mark]. **(c) How shadows form:** because light rays travel strictly in **straight lines** (rectilinear propagation) and cannot bend round solid barriers, placing an **opaque object** in front of a light source blocks rays straight ahead, creating a **dark unlit region (shadow)** directly behind it on a screen or ground [3 marks].

By contrast, *translucent* materials like frosted bathroom glass or greased paper let partial light through while scattering rays sideways so shapes appear blurred!

Always state the fundamental physical law clearly in shadow questions: **Light travels in straight lines**, so an **opaque object blocks rays** cleanly behind it.

questions.questionText:
A family wants to reduce electricity use.
- (a) State two ways of saving electricity. [2 marks]
- (b) Name one renewable energy source. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain one advantage of renewable energy. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Two ways to save electricity at home:** strictly **switching off lights, geysers, and appliances when rooms sit empty**, and replacing old hot incandescent filaments with high-efficiency **LED bulbs**, solar water heaters (*geyser timers*), or cold-water laundry cycles [2 marks]. **(b) One renewable energy source:** **solar (sunlight) photovoltaic energy, hydroelectricity (falling water), wind turbine power, or biogas** [1 mark]. **(c) Advantage of renewable energy:** renewable sources are **naturally replenished endlessly without running dry** (unlike finite coal or diesel!) and generate clean electricity with **little or no harmful carbon greenhouse gas emissions or choking air smoke** [2 marks].

Across sunny Zimbabwean schools and homesteads, rooftop solar panels powering boreholes and LED lights simultaneously lower monthly ZESA bills while keeping lighting dependable during grid load-shedding!

Pair concrete household efficiency actions cleanly with exact definitions—knowing **renewable = naturally replenished cleanly (solar/hydro/wind)** versus **non-renewable = finite fossil fuels (coal/petrol)**.

questions.questionText:
A learner investigates friction by moving objects over different surfaces.
- (a) Define friction. [1 mark]
- (b) State one useful effect. [1 mark]
- (c) State one harmful effect. [1 mark]
- (d) Explain how surface texture affects friction. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of friction:** A **contact force acting along touching surfaces that opposes sliding or rolling motion** between two objects moving (or trying to move) across each other [1 mark]. **(b) Useful effect:** rough friction grips shoe soles safely on floors for **walking without slipping**, lets **bicycle/car brakes slow tyres**, and holds knots/nails tightly [1 mark]. **(c) Harmful effect:** unwanted rubbing wears away **tractor tyres, gear teeth, and hinges**, slows moving bicycles down, and wastes useful kinetic energy as **unwanted frictional heat** [1 mark]. **(d) How surface texture affects friction:** microscopic bumps and ridges on **rough surfaces** (gravel, sandpaper) interlock deeply creating **very high friction**, whereas **smooth polished or oiled/greased surfaces** glide past with far lower interlocking resistance [2 marks].

Notice farmers rely on *both* sides daily: deep tyre treads raise traction friction in muddy fields, while smooth grease inside wheelbarrow bearings cuts harmful wear!

Remember friction is a **force opposing relative motion between touching surfaces**, increased by **roughness & heavy weight** and reduced by **smoothness, oil/grease lubrication, or ball bearings**.

questions.questionText:
A learner studies a food chain in a grassland.
- (a) Name the producer. [1 mark]
- (b) Name one consumer. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain the direction of energy transfer. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) The producer:** **Grass (or green plants)**—organisms capturing sunlight energy via photosynthesis to build food for every link above them [1 mark]. **(b) Named consumer:** **Grasshopper / zebra / impala** (*primary consumer* herbivore eating grass) or **lion / leopard** (*secondary/tertiary consumer* carnivore eating herbivores) [1 mark]. **(c) Direction of energy transfer:** energy flows **in one single direction** starting from the **Sun → Producers (grass) → Primary Consumers (herbivores) → Secondary/Tertiary Consumers (carnivores)**—arrows point strictly toward the eater, and large amounts of usable energy are lost as **warmth/heat during respiration and movement** at every step [2 marks].

Because roughly ~90% of captured energy exits as body heat or waste between trophic steps, natural savannas support vast fields of grass, smaller herds of zebras/impala, and relatively few top lions!

Check your arrows in food-chain diagrams: arrows NEVER point from lion back to zebra—arrows always show **direction energy flows (from food organism → consumer)**.

questions.questionText:
A pond becomes polluted with waste.
- (a) Name one pollutant. [1 mark]
- (b) State two effects on organisms. [2 marks]
- (c) Suggest two ways to reduce the pollution. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named water pollutant:** **raw untreated sewage, agricultural fertiliser runoff, toxic pesticides, plastic litter, or waste engine oil** [1 mark]. **(b) Two effects on aquatic organisms:** excess sewage/fertiliser runoff triggers thick surface **algal blooms** that decay and strip out **dissolved oxygen**, **suffocating fish and water insects**, while oil coats bird feathers/gills and toxic chemicals poison frogs and spread human **cholera/bilharzia** [2 marks]. **(c) Two ways to reduce water pollution:** enforce proper **waste-bin disposal/recycling** and **sewage treatment works** away from streams, alongside maintaining unploughed **vegetated riverbank buffer strips** and fixing leaking factory/tractor oil sumps [2 marks].

Clean aquatic ecosystems filter community drinking supplies naturally and supply nutritious bream/kapenta protein when farms and towns keep plastics, sewage, and toxic sprays strictly out of storm drains!

Don't stop at saying *"pollution kills fish"*—name *why* (**oxygen depletion / eutrophication**, **direct chemical toxicity**, or **clogging plastic/oil**) for full Paper 2 credit.

questions.questionText:
A learner studies the human digestive system.
- (a) Name the organ where digestion begins. [1 mark]
- (b) State one function of the stomach. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why the small intestine is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Organ where digestion begins:** **The mouth**—where teeth grind food mechanically (**mastication**) into small moist pieces while saliva’s **amylase** enzyme begins breaking starch into simple sugars chemically [1 mark]. **(b) Function of the stomach:** muscular stomach walls churn swallowed food smoothly with **hydrochloric acid** (killing swallowed germs!) and protease **pepsin enzymes** to initiate **protein breakdown** into semi-liquid chyme [1 mark]. **(c) Importance of the small intestine:** serves as both the final site of **complete chemical digestion** (breaking carbohydrates, proteins, and fats completely into soluble molecules) and the main site of **nutrient absorption** through millions of finger-like **villi** straight into the bloodstream [2 marks].

After useful nutrients cross tiny thin villi walls into blood capillaries feeding body cells, undigested roughage moves into the *large intestine* where vital water is absorbed back before egestion!

Distinguish cleanly between **Mouth (chewing + salivary starch digestion)**, **Stomach (acid germ-killing + protein digestion)**, **Small Intestine (final digestion + villi nutrient absorption)**, and **Large Intestine (water absorption)**.

questions.questionText:
A learner investigates disease prevention.
- (a) Name one communicable disease. [1 mark]
- (b) State two ways of reducing transmission. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why handwashing is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named communicable disease:** **Cholera, malaria, tuberculosis (TB), measles, typhoid, or influenza**—infectious sicknesses capable of passing directly or via vectors from person to person [1 mark]. **(b) Two transmission-reduction measures:** consistent **handwashing with clean water and soap** alongside **safe pit/flush sanitation**, childhood **immunisations**, sleeping under insecticide-treated **mosquito nets** (for malaria), or wearing masks/covering coughs cleanly [2 marks]. **(c) Why handwashing matters:** soap and running water lift and wash away invisible **bacteria and viruses** picked up on fingers after using toilets, touching shared surfaces, or handling dirty soil—stopping dangerous pathogens from entering mouths when eating or preparing family meals [2 marks].

Breaking transmission chains works far cheaper than hospitalising whole villages during rainy-season cholera outbreaks: boiling questionable borehole/well water cleanly alongside rigorous soap handwashing stops waterborne outbreaks cold!

Notice you should pair **correct disease category** (**communicable/infectious** vs non-communicable like diabetes/kwashiorkor!) with **matching prevention routes** cleanly.

questions.questionText:
A learner observes day and night.
- (a) Name the movement responsible for day and night. [1 mark]
- (b) State the approximate time Earth takes to complete one rotation. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why different places experience different times of day. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Earth movement causing day and night:** **Rotation of the Earth spinning around its own tilted North-South axis** (spinning eastward from west to east) [1 mark]. **(b) Time for one complete rotation:** **24 hours** (defining one full Earth solar day) [1 mark]. **(c) Why different places have different times:** because Earth is a curved sphere, as it spins smoothly only the **hemisphere facing the Sun experiences bright daylight** while the opposite dark side experiences **night**—causing eastern longitudes (e.g., Tokyo/Harare ahead of London/New York) to receive sunrise earlier across global **time zones** [2 marks].

Keep careful distinction between Earth’s **Rotation** on its axis (**24 hours → Day and Night**) versus Earth’s longer **Revolution** orbiting around the Sun (**365¼ days → Annual Calendar Seasons**)!

One of the classic Grade 7 Paper 2 traps is swapping **rotation** and **revolution**—lock down **"Rotation = 24 hours = Day & Night"** vs **"Revolution = 365 days = Year & Seasons"**.

questions.questionText:
A class investigates water changing state.
- (a) Name the change from liquid to gas. [1 mark]
- (b) Name the change from gas to liquid. [1 mark]
- (c) Give one example of each change in everyday life. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Liquid to gas change:** **Evaporation** (slow surface escape into invisible vapour at any warm temperature) or rapid bubbling **Boiling** throughout the liquid at 100°C [1 mark]. **(b) Gas to liquid change:** **Condensation** (warm invisible water vapour cooling down when striking cold surfaces to form tiny liquid water droplets) [1 mark]. **(c) One everyday example of each:** **Evaporation**—wet washed school uniforms drying cleanly on an outdoor clothes line under breeze and sunshine (or puddles drying off tarmac); **Condensation**—shiny liquid water droplets beading outside an ice-cold drink bottle, inside a boiling pot lid, or forming morning dew and rain clouds high in chilly sky [2 marks].

Both evaporation and condensation drive Earth’s continuous **Water Cycle**: solar heating evaporates dam and ocean water skyward, while high cold air condenses rising vapour back into visible clouds that return precious rain onto fields!

Be precise in terminology: avoid calling vapour *"steam"* loosely in physics—explain **liquid absorbs heat to evaporate** while **gas loses heat (cools) to condense** back into liquid drops.

questions.questionText:
A learner uses a microscope to observe a specimen.
- (a) State the purpose of a microscope. [1 mark]
- (b) Give one rule for handling it safely. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why very small structures can be studied with it. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Purpose of a microscope:** a precision optical instrument designed to **magnify (enlarge) invisible microscopic structures**—such as plant onion cells, blood cells, bacteria, or tiny leaf stomata—hundreds of times larger than naked human eyes can resolve [1 mark]. **(b) Safe handling rule:** always carry the microscope upright with **two steady hands** (one gripping the curved **arm**, one supporting safely beneath the heavy **base**), keep lenses clean strictly with soft **lens tissue**, and start focusing cautiously upward so glass slides never crack against lenses [1 mark]. **(c) How tiny structures become clear:** carefully curved glass **objective and eyepiece lenses refract (bend) incoming light beams** sequentially, multiplying magnification (e.g. 10× eyepiece × 40× objective = 400× enlargement) to show crisp internal organelles cleanly [2 marks].

Remember that if you ever draw magnified biology specimens in exams, you compute exact enlargement using **Magnification = Image Size ÷ Actual Size** (*M = I ÷ A*)!

Always check two practical lab habits: **two-handed carry (arm + base)** AND **focussing carefully upward using coarse knob on low power first** to avoid crushing precious glass slides.

questions.questionText:
A class tests a hypothesis by changing one factor at a time.
- (a) Define hypothesis. [1 mark]
- (b) Why should other relevant conditions be controlled? [2 marks]
- (c) State one way of recording results. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Definition of hypothesis:** A clear, **testable scientific prediction or educated explanation** stated *before* testing an experiment—for instance predicting *"Bean seedlings watered every two days will grow taller than unwatered seedlings"* [1 mark]. **(b) Why control other relevant conditions:** keeping all extra factors identical (**soil type, light exposure, seed variety, pot size, and temperature**) creates a genuine **fair test** so the scientist proves confidently that ONLY the single factor intentionally changed (**independent variable**) caused the observed difference [2 marks]. **(c) Way of recording results:** neat **labelled data tables**, **bar charts or line graphs**, and dated **observation measurement logs** showing units like millimetres or grams cleanly [1 mark].

Without holding irrelevant variables constant—imagine putting watered beans in sunny windows while hiding unwatered beans inside dark cupboards!—nobody could tell whether extra height came from water or sunlight!

Make the **fair-test rule** crystal clear in Paper 2: change **only ONE independent variable**, measure the **dependent outcome**, and hold **every control variable equal**.

questions.questionText:
A learner finds that an iron nail rusts faster in a wet place.
- (a) Name the change taking place. [1 mark]
- (b) State two conditions that encourage rusting. [2 marks]
- (c) Suggest one method of preventing rust. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Chemical change taking place:** **Rusting**—a slow irreversible chemical **oxidation** reaction converting shiny iron/steel into flaky reddish-brown iron oxide [1 mark]. **(b) Two conditions encouraging rusting:** presence of BOTH **water/moisture** AND **oxygen gas (from air)** touching exposed bare iron together (salty rain or damp farm mud speeds rust even faster!) [2 marks]. **(c) One method of preventing rust:** creating a barrier sealing air and water away from metal by **painting** gates/ox-ploughs, wiping moving parts with **oil or grease**, **galvanising** roof sheets in protective **zinc**, or storing tools strictly inside dry sheds [1 mark].

If you seal an iron nail completely inside boiled water topped with an oil layer (no oxygen!) OR inside a dry sealed jar with drying calcium chloride (no water!), the nail stays bright silver for months—proving **both oxygen and water** are simultaneously mandatory!

Rusting attacks **iron and steel specifically** (aluminium or plastic does not rust!), so list barrier protections clearly (**paint, oil/grease, zinc galvanising, dry storage**).

questions.questionText:
A learner studies magnets.
- (a) Name one material attracted by a magnet. [1 mark]
- (b) What happens when like poles are brought together? [1 mark]
- (c) State one use of magnets. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** **(a) Material attracted by a magnet:** **Iron, steel, nickel, or cobalt** (magnetic metals—not copper wire, brass, plastic, glass, or aluminium cans!) [1 mark]. **(b) Like poles brought together:** **like poles REPEL each other forcefully**—North pushes away North (*N–N*), and South pushes away South (*S–S*), whereas opposite poles (*N–S*) attract [1 mark]. **(c) Use of magnets:** guiding direction inside **magnetic compasses**, holding **fridge door seals shut**, driving electric **motors/loudspeakers/dynamos**, or separating scrap iron cans cleanly at recycling depots [1 mark].

A classic Grade 7 trap tests magnetic vs non-magnetic metals: even though **copper coins, gold rings, and aluminium pots** are shiny metals, **NONE of them stick to magnets**—only **Iron, Steel, Cobalt, and Nickel** are attracted!

Memorise the golden magnetism rhyme: **"Like poles repel, unlike poles attract"**—and remember **repulsion**, not attraction, is the surest test proving a metal bar is truly a magnet (since plain iron attracts too!).

questions.questionText:
A family wants to reduce household waste.
- (a) Define recycling. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two materials that can be recycled. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain one environmental benefit. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of recycling:** Collecting used discarded waste items (that might otherwise fill dumpsites or rivers) and **reprocessing them industrially or creatively into useful brand-new products** [1 mark]. **(b) Two recyclable materials:** **clear plastic PET bottles, aluminium drinks cans, scrap iron/copper, clean waste paper/cardboard boxes, and glass jars/bottles** [2 marks]. **(c) One environmental benefit:** drastically **cuts unsightly plastic/landfill pollution**, saves finite natural **mineral ores and forest trees**, and consumes far less electricity/coal burning than smelting new aluminium or paper from raw earth [2 marks].

Notice how recycling fits inside the famous **"3 Rs" environmental waste hierarchy** right alongside **Reduce** (buying fewer wasteful single-use plastics) and **Reuse** (refilling sturdy glass jars or tote bags many times before discarding)!

Show clear contrast in Paper 2: **Reusing** washes an existing bottle cleanly to hold seeds/water again unchanged, whereas **Recycling** melts/pulps waste material physically into new manufactured items.

questions.questionText:
A school uses computers for research and presentations.
- (a) Name one input device. [1 mark]
- (b) Name one output device. [1 mark]
- (c) State one benefit of ICT in learning. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Named computer input device:** **Keyboard, mouse, scanner, touchscreen, microphone, or webcam** (sending user commands/data *into* the computer) [1 mark]. **(b) Named output device:** **Monitor screen, laser/inkjet printer, speakers, or classroom data projector** (displaying processed results *out* to learners) [1 mark]. **(c) Benefit of ICT in learning:** expands access to **interactive educational textbooks, animated science simulations, word-processed neat assignments, spreadsheet calculations, and fast academic research** connecting rural or urban classrooms cleanly to current knowledge [2 marks].

Understanding the simple data pipeline (**Input → CPU Processing → Storage & Output**) helps learners troubleshoot cables immediately when microphones stay muted or projectors show no image!

Keep **Input (keyboard/mouse/scanner)** and **Output (monitor/printer/speakers)** strictly separate—never call a *flash drive/USB* an input/output device unless noting it is **storage media**!
